NUMERICAL AND DEVELOPMENT APPENDIX TO NEURAL BELLMAN
OPERATORS
QIAN QI
Peking University
This archival companion retains the economic models, theorems, proofs,
numerical programmes, negative results and diagnostic accounts of Neural
Bellman Operators. Current complete-catalogue and sensitivity tables are
added with their separate execution identity. Historical evidence is pre-
served, not relabeled as a new experiment. The current executable depen-
dency closure and successful records are distinct from the still-incomplete
full historical replay.

PRESERVATION

adapted reporting and their stated checks. It is not a success declaration for a later

The saved composite verifier makes 1,877,650 checks and the saved core ver-

age includes the immutable source and primary identities, cache-chain witnesses,
canonical-output equalities, the full fixed catalogue, algebraic acceptance condi-

allowance for the unchanged last-date controller. They are not presented as an
independent replay of every last-date rounded action.
The report’s protocol adapter preserves the failed frozen-code report and its
diagnostic price tables. It removes a duplicate equal keyword and matches each
16-state timing clock to the economics of those same states. The original erroneous
use of the 32-state economic cohort with those clocks is retained as a diagnostic,
with 384 old menus and 28,800 old constraints. The corrected tables contain all 384
menus, 96 complete three-clock intersections and 28,800 comparator constraints.
Neither version changes a policy, a sample, a trained actor, an original service clock
or a prespecified competitor.
The required restrictive earlier-clock sensitivity has also actually executed from

to be a subset of its current three-clock domain. The partial second earlier process
is not treated as a complete scenario. This calculation performs no retiming, new
economic query or additional population draw.

A.2. The complete statistical and cost account
The complete outcome catalogue has 174 policy cells, 116 treatment-versus- own-
control contrasts, 232 threshold-event bounds and 348 signed population compar-
isons. It uses exactly 32 independent state units. The primary and timing records
contain 5,568 and 8,352 decisions, respectively; timing repeats do not increase the
independent sample size. The simultaneous failure allocation remains 1/100 for safe
means, 1/100 for threshold events and 3/100 for signed comparisons, totaling 1/20.
Positive safe population lower bounds occur in 102 cells. None of the 348 signed
intervals is strictly positive or strictly negative. All negative, zero, unresolved and
conventional-winner comparisons remain.
All 808 paid refinement attempts completed, and all 12 qualification refusals are
charged. Zero candidate-action economic queries is a property of this enhancement
after its anchor has been qualified; it is not zero information cost for the Bellman
problem. Complete clocks retain historical acquisition, fitting, finite-training audits,
rejected candidates, certificate arithmetic, loading, inference and process overhead.
The full research ledger separately records independent validation, report construc-
tion, failures, recovery, source checking and publication. The reporter’s field headed
actual_new_scientific_stage_seconds_excluding_current_report is only its pri-
mary/canonical/statistics subtotal. It omits prior continuation segments and cache
checks and is never used as a full study total. The interrupted primary and indepen-
dent parents lack exact terminal clocks; their completed measured work remains
a lower bound. Overlapping parent and child clocks are not added. Shared-host
timings are not a dedicated-hardware performance benchmark.

The following eight pages contain the complete fixed-order catalogue, including
the online controls and every representation, budget and fitting loss. Gain panels use
32 state units. Work panels use the matching first 16 states in each of three original
timing processes. Common acquired information cancels only in the displayed
paired difference; complete levels and all allocations remain in the numerical tables.

APPENDIX E: ACTION-ALIGNED ACQUISITION AND COMPLETE-POLICY WORK
A continuation is acquired to make a decision, not to minimize an approximation
statistic in isolation. The retained investment experiment makes the distinction op-
erational: every certificate-oriented fit reduces its validated residual span, whereas
aggregate first-proposal rejections increase. We now construct an acquisition target
in the units of the admission inequality. The construction uses the same original
action set and risk law as the NBO policy account.

APPENDIX F: RESOLVING THE ACTIVE INNOVATION TAILS
The original continuous innovation law supplies information that an NBO must
share with its strongest conventional competitors. Convexity of a continuation along
that innovation implies that the adverse outcomes occupy at most two endpoint
intervals. Locating these intervals before quadrature changes which continuation
values must be acquired. In particular, the upper information bound need not pay a
factor (1 −α)−1 for resolving the entire innovation support when only a fraction
1 −α is adverse. The result below is a deterministic point-information theorem and
an outward Bellman implementation. It does not assert a neural representation
separation, a randomized optimum, or multivariate tractability.

consists of exact point values, the original uniform law, and these class restrictions.

and L = 2Rα for 0 < α < 1, and let I = [−R, R −L]. For u ∈I put

The conclusion applies to boundary proposals, a one-sided tail, a nonoptimal tail cut, a
rounded action, and an imperfect stored continuation used only to generate the proposal. It
requires neither convexity of the implemented policy value nor differentiation through the
rounded terminal actor. With the same proposal and the same future policy, a different valid
certificate changes information about cost, not the cost itself.
A cut obtained from the stored critic can be a useful proposal, but the tail defect
in (A.14) must concern the original V1. The same fixed feasible tail density supplies
the all-action minorant; it is never differentiated as though it were an exact opti-
mizer. The new service and the uniform-support conventional service both pay
for tail proposals, original terminal evaluations, refused certificates, refinement,
and fallback. Operation savings and actual returned-policy contrasts are reported
separately.
F.3. Paid precision and recursive use
For any finite list of attempted resolutions, accepting at the first resolution whose
outward intervals meet both original targets preserves qualification. Every un-
successful earlier attempt remains part of the service cost. A geometric ladder
alone gives no promise that a rejected action ever qualifies: its limiting support-
ing quadratic may remain too loose, or the action itself may be too costly. The
unchanged fallback therefore remains part of the delivered policy.
For a declared fixed graph with exact-value quadrature allowance A/n2, tail-
localization allowance B4−m, A, B > 0, positive costs cqn + cbm, and usable tolerance
ϵ > 0 after all other errors have been charged, an interior continuous optimum
satisfies

compute price or a globally optimal discovery policy. Its proof is in the supplement.

H.3. Proof for pathwise-sound random intervals
Use the same fixed f0 as above, before drawing a random tape. Outside the single
null set in the soundness definition, fixing the tape gives a deterministic adaptive
procedure that is sound for all inputs. The preceding chord construction therefore
forces the stated width on its transcript from f0. The chord competitor may vary
with the tape; f0 does not. Taking expectation gives the same lower bound on
expected width. A procedure whose bad-tape set depends on the input need not be
sound for that tape’s chord competitor, which is why the argument proves no such
assertion for ordinary 1 −δ coverage.
Q.E.D.

VALUE GRADIENTS, BOUNDARIES AND IMPLEMENTATION AUTHORITY:
The
expanded Q1 is continuously differentiable in (x, a); its positive-part square and the
tail function are C1 at their junctions. Set a = A(x)u with u ∈[0,1]. The transformed
objective has a unique minimizing u because A(x) > 0 and the action objective is
strictly convex. Continuity of this minimizer follows directly by taking convergent
subsequences in the compact interval and passing the minimizing inequality to the
limit; uniqueness makes every subsequential limit the same. For a state increment h,
compare values using the old optimizer for an upper bound and the new optimizer
for a lower bound. Differentiability of the objective and continuity of the optimizer
squeeze the value increment to [∇xQ1 + u∂aQ1∇A]Th + o(∥h∥). At an interior
optimum ∂aQ1 = 0; at zero u = 0; and at capacity u = 1 with ∂aQ1 ≤0. This proves
(A.41), its continuity and its one-sided boundary version. Inside a smooth region
with strict interiority, differentiating the zero action derivative and using ∂aaQ1 ≥2
proves the implicit actor derivative. The strict endpoint regions have the stated
actor formulas. At junctions the value argument still holds, but no actor derivative
is required.
The implementation does not claim exact evaluation of this symbolic root. It
rounds a floating proposal to the inherited action quantum, verifies feasibility and
evaluates the same original feasible risk witness as in Proposition 4. Its lower bound
pays the full multiplier residual and interval uncertainty, and its upper bound
encloses the original objective. If its gap fails the inherited threshold, the old certified
oracle is called and charged. Each branch therefore returns an original-value bracket
and a valid global state support. The context manager changes bindings for optimal-
continuation calls only and restores them on exceptions. It does not replace the
actual terminal controller or its error allowance in complete-policy evaluation.
Thus all original-policy enclosures remain those of Theorem 5; an unverified cubic

APPENDIX K: TAIL-SWITCH ACCURACY AND ITS ECONOMIC MEANING
PROOF OF THEOREM A.15:
We first justify the derivatives rather than differ-
entiating a sorting permutation. For an outcome Ya, write AVaRα(Ya) = minη{η +
t−1E(Ya −η)+}. The unique quantile minimizes this expression. At the anchor,
absence of mass at that quantile and dominated action derivatives give the ac-
tion derivative of the minimized expression, with the quantile held fixed, as
t−1E[1{Ya>ηY}∇aYa]. To verify the envelope step, local L1 continuity bounds the
relevant minimizing quantiles in a compact interval. Any convergent subsequence
of minimizers has to minimize the limiting continuous objective; uniqueness forces
convergence to the anchor quantile. Comparing the two minimized objectives at
each other’s minimizers then gives the derivative formula by dominated conver-
gence. Equivalently the unique tail density gives the same supporting derivative.
The domination and uniqueness hypotheses in the statement are used at precisely
these steps.
Let eH = Ha + c and denote its quantile by eη. The almost-sure inequalities eH −ϵ ≤
Za ≤eH + ϵ imply |η −eη| ≤ϵ by the monotonicity and translation rule of the
generalized quantile. Put E = {Za > η} and F = { eH > eη}. Both have probability t.
If Za > η + 2ϵ, then eH > η + ϵ ≥eη, so the point lies in both upper tails. If Za < η −2ϵ,
then eH < η −ϵ ≤eη, so it lies in neither. Hence E △F ⊆Bϵ up to null sets. Since
P(E) = P(F) = t, its mass is at most 2min(t,1 −t) as well as P(Bϵ).

EXACT COUNTEREXAMPLE:
For z uniform on [−1,1], its upper half-tail mean
is 1/2 and its lower half-tail mean is −1/2. Consequently AVaR1/2(kz) = |k|/2.
On the stated action interval the true objective is a2 + (a + 1)/2 and the surrogate
is a2 + (1 −a)/2. Each is strictly convex, with derivatives 2a + 1/2 and 2a −1/2,
respectively. Their feasible minimizers are −1/4 and 1/4. Completing the first
square gives a loss (1/4 + 1/4)2 = 1/4. Direct integration of the two affine tails
gives the same values. Nevertheless ∂aZa = ∂aHa = z. The different maximizing
densities, not a pointwise derivative error, produce the wrong decision.
Q.E.D.
APPENDIX L: COMPLETE-INCUMBENT AND RECURSIVE IMPROVEMENT
PROOF OF PROPOSITION A.17:
The interval premises imply J −J′ ≥l −u′ > 0
at every accepted gate. If a trial is refused, the complete incumbent action and future
policy are retained exactly. Induction over the finite trace gives weak decrease from
the completed starting policy, with a strict decrease whenever a gate is accepted.
The added qualification predicate holds for the starting policy and for each accepted
replacement, so induction also preserves both original targets. This reasoning uses
actual policy costs, not their regret upper bounds. It supplies no comparison to an
unexecuted baseline or to a controller with a different future policy.
Q.E.D.

The maps P± are monotone, preserve constants, and are nonexpansive; hence the
two gain maps are contractions. Iterating each comparison at D and passing to its
fixed point proves D−≤D ≤D+. Iterating the lower gain map from zero proves
D−≥0. These are robust discounted gain accounts; identifying them with physical
occupation measures would discard the original risk envelope.
For the successive policies, safe improvement gives Jπk+1 ≤Jπk and, more pre-
cisely, Jπk+1 ≤Tπk+1 Jπk. The additional greedy inequality and contraction of T imply

N.4. Paid precision and conditional allocation
PROOF: Qualification at a chosen stage of a finite sequence follows from its own
verified inequalities; no monotonicity of earlier reported widths is needed. Summing
the actual cost of every attempted stage is the complete cost. If a deterministic ladder
has work cnj per stage with nj = 2jn0, its total work through nJ is less than 2cnJ.
Such a bound requires this work model and does not remove fixed costs, descendant
solves, refused trials, or rational fallback.

APPENDIX O: QUALIFICATION AND WORK OF THE BOUNDED PRELIMINARY
SERVICE
O.1. Objects, information, and algorithm
Fix a state x, its original feasible action interval [0, A(x)], a realized proposal
a ∈[0, A(x)], and α ∈{1/2,3/4}. Write
R = 1/32,
t = 1 −α,
L = 2Rα,
I = [−R, R −L],
fa(z) = V1(F(x, a, z)).
The primitive transition is affine in the innovation and the action. The already
established original bounds give convexity of fa, its strong-convexity modulus
mz = 181/64, and V1 ≤J1 ≤V1 + ε1 for the implemented terminal controller, with
ε1 = 2−20. Its complete-policy cost is
J(a) = S(x) + h(a) + β AVaRα(J1 ◦Fa),
whereas Q(a) uses V1 in this expression, and V0(x) = inf0≤v≤A(x) Q(v).
Two information types are distinguished. A floating terminal value is used only
to propose a cut. An outward terminal payload encloses the original V1 value; when
used at a quadrature midpoint it also supplies a valid global affine minorant, with
every uncertain slope component retained. These are the same original payloads
used by the common terminal compiler. Counting a payload does not assign unit
cost to its internal original-risk evaluation, optimization, interval arithmetic, or
supporting-witness construction.
The floating proposal compares fa(u + L) −fa(u) at the two endpoints of I. A
proposed endpoint exit suppresses further floating search for that row. Otherwise
six interval-halving updates are performed, after which the midpoint of the final
proposed bracket is rounded and clipped to the feasible 2−32 grid. The signs need
not be correct: only feasibility of the final cut u is used below. The production
domain checks enforce this feasibility and the declared risk levels.

All preliminary values are counted.
The two floating endpoint differences request
four terminal values per proposed action, including any repeated locations. Only
rows without a proposed endpoint exit receive further queries. Six such updates
request two values each, so their total is at most 4 + 6 · 2 = 16; a proposed endpoint
exit uses four.
The outward defect requests exactly two values once for that state/action/risk
identity. A resolution with m cells in each of p nonempty tails uses pm midpoint
payloads and p(m + 1) endpoint payloads, hence p(2m + 1). The calculation allows
repeated locations across resolutions, between a midpoint and an earlier endpoint,
and between the defect and quadrature. All such repeated calls remain charged. A
first-resolution acceptance thus uses at most 2 + 5p outward payloads. If the second
resolution is attempted, the complete preliminary total is
2 + p{(2 · 2 + 1) + (2 · 4 + 1)} = 2 + 14p ≤30.
The cache is why the two defect values are not reacquired at the second resolution.
Grouping rows according to their positive tails changes the number of vector calls,
not these scalar-payload counts. An earlier failed call cannot enlarge the prescribed
subsequent schedule; it terminates with a failed record instead of licensing an
unrecorded retry.

O.3. Ablation and prospective scope
The masked-tail ablation uses the same proposal, cache, exact zero-mass omission,
original bounds, and fallback, while attempting all m ∈{2,4,8,16,32,64}. The

even if the later fallback is identical.
These two schedules were chosen after the separately preserved Phase A results
and are therefore declared as Phase B algorithm development. The five-service com-
parison reacquires the common training information and executes its conventional
controls and original-policy reference enclosures afresh under its own source freeze.
Neither the mathematical validity of early acceptance nor the information cap es-
tablishes lower elapsed time, lower policy regret, a calibrated adoption decision,
or neural specificity. Those claims require the corresponding current records. In
particular, early acceptance may keep an actor proposal that another service repairs;
its complete original-policy cost must be evaluated as that returned policy, with the
unchanged future controller.
Packing the same original point information.
At a fixed attempted resolution, index
every positive-weight midpoint request and every endpoint request of a positive-
length tail by its original row, column, and request type. Concatenating these indices
defines a bijection to a packed list. A packed entry retains the original state xi, action
ai, and innovation zi and requests the same original payload at F(xi, ai, zi). Distinct
requests at an identical location remain separate paid entries. The inverse indices
return the lower values, endpoint upper values, and supporting slopes to precisely
their original summands.
Conditional on a given valid collection of original payloads, this operation is
only a reindexing of the selected-tail lower sum, secant upper sum, and all-action
supporting slope. A zero-length tail has zero weights, so its omitted terms can be
represented by zeros without asserting that the unobserved continuation equals

account. When w = 0, D = m is constant; cash invariance gives risk difference
m exactly and avoids an empty zero-slack set when the original supremum is
unattained. A loose bracket with positive width can also be used in that case, at the
price of a weaker bound.

Q.7. Proof of the result A.74
PROOF: At r = 1, analytic endpoint enclosures and the minorant lemma give the
assertion. Suppose it holds for r −1. Each child interval encloses the true optimal
continuation. If the numerical next state is an interval, expanding the queried center
value by Gr−1 times the maximum ℓ1 displacement encloses all its possible values.
Conditional-mean lower bounds and the semiconcavity remainder then give valid
endpoint brackets for the true Qr. The minorants cover the entire action interval.
A downward capacity endpoint can omit only an interval of length equal to the
certified capacity-rounding difference; subtracting Λr times that difference accounts
for its possible improvement. The minimum upper endpoint is the cost of a feasible
first action followed by the optimal future. This proves (i) by induction. Retaining
earlier valid lower bounds preserves every conclusion.
For termination, an interval of length h has minorant at least its smaller lower end-
point minus Hrh2/8. Its smaller upper endpoint is an available global upper bound.

made by a prediction, disjoint terminal fragments consequently have total number

budget. Bounded action-quantum rounding of a proposed quarter-to-three-quarter

Otherwise precision must be increased; a fixed-precision run is not allowed to
ignore this requirement.

Q.8. Proof of the result A.64
PROOF: A routed action is merely another feasible partition point. The endpoint
and minorant induction in Theorem A.74 therefore applies without change. After
each evaluation retain the smallest upper endpoint and the maximum of the old and
newly valid global lower endpoints. Their difference cannot increase. The stopping
test uses this difference, not a fitted value or a prediction error.
Put hδ = √
3δ/Hr. A partition interval of length at most hδ has minimum mino-
rant at least its smaller lower endpoint minus 3δ/8. The associated upper endpoint,
with the stipulated width and capacity allowance, is within δ of that minorant.
Such an interval cannot be responsible for an unresolved global gap. Every split
parent therefore has length greater than hδ. The one-fifth condition makes each of
its children longer than hδ/5. Starting with one interval, disjoint terminal fragments
consequently number at most 1 + 5c(x)/hδ. Counting endpoints and allowing for
rounding of this numerical bound gives the displayed conservative budget. Floating
failure is handled by the separately charged exact-rational procedure, not by this
real-arithmetic count.
The first assertion about predictor evaluation follows from the order of the stop-
ping test and the routing rule. For the last assertion, use backward induction on
the remaining horizon, with the common analytic terminal kernel as base. At each
nonterminal query, declined predictions leave the same conventional split, lower
bound, witness and tie rule. Induction over partition refinements gives the same
next query and returned endpoints; the induction over dates then gives the same
implemented policy. Model-evaluation work can still differ, so transcript identity is
not a zero-cost fitting claim.

Q.10. Proof of the result A.61
PROOF: For each drawn bin sequence, conditional integration over its continu-
ous realizations places the exact path expectation between the interval endpoints.
Uniform mixing over the equal bins recovers the original continuous law. The lower
endpoint expectation is thus no larger than Di, and the upper endpoint expectation
is no smaller. Apply the bounded empirical-Bernstein inequality of Maurer and
Pontil (2009) to the endpoint samples and take the union bound, with outward
arithmetic included in the mean, variance and radius. Conditional validity for every
H implies unconditional validity by integration. On this one simultaneous event, all
ensuing deterministic comparisons of the covered quantities hold together. Q.E.D.

PROOF: Subtract the gain intervals from k and compare the resulting interval
endpoints with zero. Taking the image of [l, u] under the absolute-value map gives
(A.144). The assertions hold simultaneously for every nonnegative fee on the origi-
nal coverage event.

APPENDIX R: ACTION COMPARISONS THAT CAN CHANGE THE INVESTMENT
DECISION
An accurate continuation approximation contributes economically when it helps
choose a better feasible action at an acceptable complete cost. The retained R119
service experiments kept the implemented actions fixed. We now construct an
action comparison whose acquisition error decreases with the distance between the
actions, and use it to safeguard actual policy changes. The original nested AVaR
criterion, information available to the economic agent, capacity constraint, and
future controller remain those in Section 5.

at these midpoints and endpoints. Let La, Lb be their weighted midpoint lower

∑i wi{ fb(zi) −fa(zi)} using the paired midpoint intervals. All of these acquisitions,
including both action payloads, are paid.

R.1. Safe refinement, stopping, and the future-policy floor
Start from a completed original-policy incumbent. A proposed replacement is
accepted only when the upper endpoint of (A.29) is strictly negative and its own
policy interval passes the unchanged regret target τ = 1/256 and width target
1/8192. At the same state an original-optimum lower bound may be reused across
actions; an action’s policy interval may not. Refuse a candidate when its lower
contrast endpoint is nonnegative, or retain the incumbent when the prespecified
work limit is exhausted. Every refused trial remains in the complete cost.

Outward square roots in the transferred bound.
The implementation intersects the
directly acquired incumbent deficit with an outward version of the transfer bound.
For an exact nonnegative rational z = p/q with q > 0, let m be the integer square
root of ⌊280p/q⌋, and increase m by one if m2q < 280p. The resulting m/240 is at
least √z: before a possible increment, m is the floor of 240√z, and the exact square
comparison detects whether that floor was exact. A binary64 conversion is moved
upwards when its exact rational value is smaller than the dyadic bound, and its
squared exact rational value is checked against z. Applying this procedure to upper
endpoints, followed by outward additions, products, and squaring, gives a valid
transferred deficit. Taking the smaller of two valid upper bounds remains valid.
Both direct endpoint payloads and all integer operations are still paid. Because this
is an incumbent-deficit bound, its tightening directly affects the lower contrast and
the certified-refusal predicate; it does not itself tighten the candidate-deficit term in
the upper acceptance endpoint.

suffice.

T.2. Interpretation and the remaining cost obligation
Every mathematical implication above holds for the original economic state
where its inequalities are established. Population statements require their separately
specified sampling and inference assumptions. Finite training labels alone do not
establish uniform coverage, and a uniform conservative bound does not demon-
strate that its construction is affordable. The complete cost comparison must pay
for the original-Q value bundles, every probe, basis construction, bounded value
fit, marginal LP, exact primal–dual verification, feature ranges, action extraction,
rejected certification and the complete accepted policy service. Any scientific refer-
ence calculation is identified separately and cannot be presented as free deployment
work.
The derivative target eliminates neither the original tail integration nor the
unchanged-future floor in (10). It makes their placement explicit: the original risk
integration is paid before fitting, the action-relevant training objective is minimized
over a stated finite class, and the future allowance is applied to an implemented
policy after the original-Q calculation. The matched hinge, polynomial, spline, grid
and semi-analytic methods have the same access to this construction. A conclusion
about neural adoption, scalability or an applied economic calibration therefore still
requires its corresponding complete-cost and economic evidence.

APPENDIX V: INTRODUCTION
A dynamic decision maker buys an approximation because it changes the cost
of making a good decision. In a constrained investment problem, an accurate
continuation level can still give the wrong incentive to invest, while a continuation
with a large common level error can choose the correct action. Under recursive
risk, the difficulty is greater: changing a continuation can also change which shocks
receive adverse weight. A numerical method must therefore connect its acquired
information, its fitted critic, its feasible actor and its computational work to the
original recursive objective.
Neural Bellman Operators (NBOs) address this chain by constructing and learn-
ing recursive continuation operators together with an account of their policy error.
The object is the Bellman operator of the specified economy. Its criterion, infor-
mation filtration, constraints and boundary conditions remain part of that object
throughout approximation and deployment. The paper retains both a constructive
own-future neural operator and an analysis of arbitrary acquired critics. It develops
their links with stochastic control and, under separate explicit assumptions, nonlin-
ear Brownian recursive utility. A result for the nested risk investment application is
not automatically a welfare improvement in a different expected-utility or nonlinear
recursive-utility model.
The central computational question is which continuation information is worth
acquiring. Earlier NBO calculations found a concrete mismatch: every certificate-
oriented fit in a retained comparison reduced a residual-span criterion, but the aggre-
gate number of rejected first actions increased from 644 to 757. The quadratic control
remained a strong complete-service baseline. The subsequent policy-comparison
calculations preserved that economic criterion and constructed safe actual improve-
ments, yet acquisition still used a value loss. Those results motivate a new learning
calculation in the original model. Their observations and costs retain their historical
identities in the development companion; the present sample does not reuse them.
We learn the marginal continuation cost after evaluating the original risk operator.
This order matters. In the two-date investment economy, the original optimal
continuation is the last-date Bellman image of the known terminal function. It is

acquired through paid outward calculations. The root critic retains the known action
cost and learns the action-dependent part of the integrated continuation. A state-
only anchor completes its value level. The resulting actor is proposed by piecewise
minimization of that learned objective over the original capacity interval. Floating
critical-point calculations generate a proposal; admission requires a certificate for
the original complete policy. The same acquired values, features where relevant,
feasible actions and certification rules are available to the conventional controls.
The mathematical contribution has three connected parts. First, we derive a con-
tinuous original-action marginal and explicit moduli from the nonlinear investment
technology, binding capacity and moving AVaR tails. The central interval excluded
from the adverse tail can touch either shock boundary. Its variational inequalities
control movement of the tail without differentiating a numerical sort or an un-
constrained optimizer. Finite original-risk value enclosures then provide outward
derivative labels, with the precision cost of finite differences paid explicitly.
Second, a bounded readout is fitted to minimize the worst action-marginal dis-
crepancy over those outward labels. The finite training problem is convex for each
declared feature family. Exact primal and dual bounds certify the actual stored
coefficients without treating a floating solver’s success flag as a proof. An explicit
feature-range construction states how to extend the acquired information to off-
design action comparisons. Its integral along the feasible action path controls policy
loss and possible policy changes; a capacity-sensitive stationarity bound sharpens
the account when available. The argument applies to a nonconvex fitted polyno-
mial or spline through the all-action comparison, and never assumes that target
smoothness removes a fitted ReLU kink. This extension is a proved construction
whose numerical cell bounds and cost must also be supplied before it can certify an
off-design decision. The current experiment audits the finite-node fits and admits
policies through the separate original-model certificate; it does not claim to have
executed that global feature-cell calculation.
Third, we state what is lost if the critic’s anchor is discarded recursively. In
this very investment transition, a state-dependent continuation level that does not
change a last-date action can shift the root marginal by a known nonzero amount.
A full level-and-contrast recursion therefore carries the anchor error, the action gap

and the future policy error separately. A noncash-invariant recursive preference
receives its own continuation Lipschitz account. It cannot inherit a monetary shift

Derivative-assisted economic dynamic programming already uses Hermite ap-
proximation with value and slope information (Cai and Judd, 2015). Derivative
supervision and task-based model learning also have established precedents (Czar-
necki et al., 2017, Donti et al., 2017, Elmachtoub and Grigas, 2022). The training
certificates use convex duality and affine supporting bounds; these general tools do
not themselves supply a claim of methodological novelty. The development history
also contains certificate-aware readouts and an action-null quotient analysis. The
additional results here concern their explicit construction and verification for the
original recursive risk operator, including tail changes, paid finite-risk information,
feasible actions and recursive value levels. A three-probe lower bound identifies
a limitation of that stated information interface; it is not a lower bound for every
algorithm with access to the investment formulas.
The numerical comparison changes the learning loss before changing the evalua-
tion sample. Two separately executed acquisition budgets use nested state designs.
Seven stored representations each have a value-loss and an action-marginal-loss
critic; the online original-model method is included at both risk levels. Quadratic,
polynomial, cubic spline, multilinear grid and semi-analytic controls form the
conventional menu. An exactly corresponding hinge encoding makes the neural
representation claim testable: a geometry shared with that control is not a uniquely
neural contribution.
The protocol fixes 64 new independent initial states, complete original-policy
evaluation, five fresh matched timing processes, exact independent reconstruction,
simultaneous positive and adverse gain inference and full acquisition/service cost
comparisons. It also fixes how unresolved and failed calculations are retained. The
empirical question is whether action-marginal learning changes decisions, rejections
and complete work enough to compensate for its acquisition cost. A reduction of its
own finite-node fitting objective alone does not answer that question.
The completed comparison gives an adverse answer for the implemented learner.

The main article presents the economic operator, its original-risk qualification
and the new learning construction. The supplement contains complete proofs and
retains the earlier action, tail-information and policy improvement theorems. The
development companion preserves the earlier applications, numerical records,
negative findings and source-bound revision history. This organization keeps the
active economic and mathematical argument readable while retaining the research
needed to assess it.

W.1. The original decision and the acquired information
The original model is (13)–(14) at d = 2, two dates and risk levels 1/2 and 3/4.
Investment raises the two next-date stocks by a/2 and a/4, whereas the continuous
innovation shifts them by (z,−z). It therefore changes the stocks’ imbalance without
changing their aggregate. The decision trades the current adjustment cost against
tracking, the low-stock penalty, capacity and the original risk-sensitive continuation.
All objective quantities below use the original normalized cost units; the experiment
has no monetary or consumption-equivalent calibration.
Two endpoint state grids have 52 and 92 states. Each buys five normalized-
action derivative contexts and their fixed feasible probes, or thirteen original-value
contexts per state. The protocol requires a separate actual acquisition process for
each budget. Every method within it receives the same complete information bundle
and is charged for its declared standalone acquisition. The optimized last-date
continuation is acquired from the original known terminal primitives. It is neither a
free oracle nor a target supplied by another representation. The root critic learns the
original integrated continuation difference; its separately stored state-only anchor
completes the value level. The future deployed controller is unchanged, with β2−20
charged once in a complete-policy upper bound.

W.3. Independent reconstruction and the statistical unit
The source/protocol commit precedes all acquisition. The acquired model commit
precedes a single new operating-system entropy draw. The state commit precedes
every outcome. There are 58 policy cells, 3,712 primary singleton decisions and
9,280 decisions in five serial fresh timing processes. The independent economic
reconstruction evaluates all distinct final-policy and raw-proposal keys with the
same rational design, and the separate training audit reconstructs the actual al-
gebraic feature rows and finite-box gaps. The 64 states, rather than risk cells or
repeated clocks, are the independent statistical units. Their population is the prod-
uct uniform law on the two 40-bit initial-state coordinates, conditional on the stated
independent OS-entropy assumption. The original innovation distribution remains
continuous. Independent validation reconstructs optimized-continuation values
with exact rational primitive formulas and adds the implemented-future allowance
once; compatibility with a production interval does not by itself certify that inter-
val’s narrower endpoints.
Gain is original cost under VALUE minus original cost under MARGINAL on
the same state. It can have either sign. Both completed policies have regret in
[0,1/256], so a paired gain lies in [−1/256,1/256]. The fixed joint 95 percent family
in Proposition A.13 includes the two optimal-value means, all 58 policy-regret
means, all 28 signed loss contrasts, 112 signed threshold probabilities and both
endpoints of all 58 first-rejection probabilities. Identical policy keys cancel exactly
without creating new sample units. Raw proposals have no final-service regret cap;
their complete sample diagnostics are reported separately. Cross-family sample
comparisons and compute-price regions do not acquire an undeclared population-
superiority interpretation.

APPENDIX X: LEARNING THE ORIGINAL ACTION MARGINAL: COMPLETED

The experiment changes the fitted original Bellman critic. VALUE and
MARGINAL use the same paid original-law value probes, the same anchored fea-
tures, coefficient boxes and feasible proposal rule within each budget. MARGINAL
is fitted to minimize the finite-node robust action-marginal loss; VALUE is fitted to
minimize bounded value least squares. Both fitting calculations retain their actual
independently bounded optimization gaps. The trained critic proposes an action,
and the unchanged original-model service qualifies the complete policy. Thus a
smaller training loss and a better original economic decision are distinct outcomes.
All 56 stored actors and the online comparator were fixed before the new 64-row
initial-state sample. The completed study contains all 58 risk–policy cells, 3,712
primary decisions and 9,280 decisions in five fresh serial timing processes. Both
risks share the same 64 initial states; neither timing repeats nor the equal-feature
hinge encoding increase the number of independent observations. The innovation
distribution remains continuous and the original future controller is unchanged.
The independent primitive implementation evaluated 1,301 distinct exact state–
action–risk keys, including every available first proposal and every final policy,
using 167,829 terminal contexts. Its fixed 64-cell enclosures reconstruct original
optimized-continuation values and add the unchanged β2−20 future-policy al-
lowance once. Agreement with production intervals is compatibility; it does not
certify the production compiler’s narrower endpoints. All final production policies
qualified at regret target 1/256 and interval-width target 1/8192. The largest saved
production regret upper bound was 0.0038604, and the largest recorded interval
width was 0.00000286.

X.2. What the learning calculation certifies
The exact independent finite-design audit found a smaller stored-coefficient
marginal residual for MARGINAL in 28 of the 28 treatments, equality in 0, and a
larger residual in 0. It reconstructs the feature and derivative design with rational
arithmetic, checks the 30-bit coefficients and boxes, and bounds the finite-box
optimum using valid rational dual weights. The marginal optimality-gap upper
bounds range from 0.0000000 to 0.0000001; the corresponding VALUE least-squares
gap upper bounds range from 0.0000000 to 0.0002331. The complete per-model
results include floating-design discrepancies and both losses evaluated at every
actual stored coefficient vector.
These finite-node optimization statements establish the implemented fitting calcu-
lation. A global feature-cover bound was not numerically established by this experi-
ment, and a small node residual is not a substitute for the separate original-law pol-
icy certificate. The two grids measure paid information and feature-budget changes
within this two-state, two-date economy. They do not provide state-dimension,
horizon or innovation-dimension scaling evidence.
The ReLU and hinge controls have identical fixed features and stored readouts.
In the primary records, 512 of 512 paired final actions and 512 paired raw proposals
were identical. All five timing comparisons are retained separately. Hinge pays
the corresponding full ReLU fitting charge plus its own identity, encoding and
audit costs. It is a conventional equal-feature control, not an independent fit or
an additional independent scientific outcome; shared geometry cannot establish a
neural-exclusive representation advantage.

For the prespecified reuse volumes N ∈{64,256,1024,16384}, the deployment
scenario is Cm(N) = Am + Hm + Lm + (N/n)(Tm −Lm). Here Am is the allocated
acquisition and training-audit cost, Hm the stated common process residual, Lm
the cold load, and Tm the measured complete cohort. The primary scenario has
n = 64 and matching 64-state economics; each timing scenario has n = 32 and
matching first-32 economics. Independent all-policy research validation is reported
separately and excluded from this deployment-reuse formula. Reuse is a specified
amortization calculation, not measured throughput.

objective units per measured second. A sufficient price domain requires the lower

choice remain unresolved.
X.4. Economic interpretation under the original criterion
The adverse mean gains concern the deployed decisions in the same investment
economy. The relevant incentive combines the known marginal adjustment cost
h′(a) with the original risk-integrated continuation marginal. Correct boundary
signs can justify no investment or a capacity action; an interior decision needs their
balance at the chosen state and action. Minimizing the largest discrepancy at the
acquired nodes does not by itself control that balance off design or the integrated
contrast between competing actions. Theorem S.7 and Proposition S.8 make those
additional requirements explicit. The campaign has not isolated how much of the
adverse performance comes from label width, the allocation of approximation error
across nodes, or the fitted geometry away from them. Assigning the outcome to
any one of these mechanisms would require a further independently specified
comparison.

The refusal records show a direct consequence for the decision service. Across
the two risks and budgets, VALUE incurs 60 first rejections and MARGINAL incurs
294, out of 1,792 proposals each. These are catalogue counts; matched hinge policies
do not add independent observations. Every one of the 354 refusals triggers a
paid conventional fallback and changes the deployed action. The final adverse
mean gains in Table X.I already include that correction. Thus qualification protects
the declared policy-loss ceiling while leaving substantial differences in attained
economic accuracy and total work. The original-action RMS quantities in Table AA.I
remain upper bounds inferred from curvature, not exact measured action errors.
The online original-model control has a strictly lower independently enclosed
64-state mean cost than each of the 56 learned cells in the saved paired compar-
isons. Its mean regret upper bounds are 1.88 × 10−6 and 2.04 × 10−6 at risk levels
1/2 and 3/4. A strong conventional approximation can get much closer to that
accuracy than the tested neural critic. At budget 9, VALUE spline mean regret lies
in [1.10,3.29] × 10−6 and [4.61,7.08] × 10−6 at the two risks; MARGINAL ReLU
regret lies in [381.99,384.17] × 10−6 and [470.95,473.34] × 10−6. These are outward
sample enclosures under the original criterion. They are neither welfare estimates
for another preference model nor population rankings across representations.
Acquisition changes the economically relevant cost comparison. At N = 64, the
online control’s allocated complete costs are 10.108 and 10.846 seconds, below every
learned alternative at the corresponding risk. Amortization can make conventional
approximation useful at larger declared reuse volumes. For example, at N = 16384
the coarse VALUE spline costs 510.208 and 470.272 seconds in the primary-clock
scenario, against 1193.379 and 1382.227 for the online method, while retaining
a higher original sample cost. These are calculations under the stated reuse for-
mula, not observed throughput. Their economic relevance depends on the price
of computation and the accepted accuracy tradeoff. The entire conventional menu,
every clock and all four volumes enter the price tests; a favorable comparison with
a selected rival does not establish adoption against that menu. Each of the 192
ReLU primary-or-individual-clock volume scenarios has a conventional sample
dominator in the saved cost-frontier table.

The larger acquisition budget is also not a monotone policy improvement. It buys
81/25 times as many original-value contexts per risk, with allocated acquisition and
audit charges about 2.53–2.77 times as large. Of the 28 fine-versus-coarse sample
contrasts, 15 favor the finer budget, 12 favor the coarser budget and one remains
unresolved. MARGINAL ReLU improves at risk 1/2 but worsens at risk 3/4; its
first rejections respectively rise from 10 to 14 and fall from 13 to 10. Table AA.VI
retains all contrasts. These changes show why neither denser acquisition nor a
lower refusal count can replace direct measurement of original economic loss. They
concern two information budgets in the same economy, with no state-dimension or
horizon extrapolation.
Statewise outcomes vary within the adverse mean comparison. At the prespec-
ified threshold 2−20, the fixed joint 95 percent event family gives positive lower
bounds on the probability of a benefit in 26 of 28 treatments and of harm in all 28.
At threshold 2−16 the corresponding counts are 25 and 28. These separate event
statements coexist with unresolved population mean gains. The independent com-
parisons were not used to select the deployed actions. A deployable rule that
chooses a statewise improvement must acquire valid original-objective contrast
bounds before making that choice and pay for them, as required by Theorem S.7.
No gain, service cost or adoption region is credited to such an unexecuted selector.
APPENDIX Y: ECONOMIC USE AND THE REMAINING RESEARCH TASK
The role of a Neural Bellman Operator is to acquire and reuse continuation
information that changes feasible economic decisions at an acceptable total cost.
The new construction supplies original-marginal regularity, paid derivative labels,
checked finite-box fitting gaps and sufficient action conditions under the original
recursive risk objective. The implemented MARGINAL learner nevertheless raises
the independently enclosed sample mean cost in every loss comparison, and its
timing improvements are a minority of the complete records. This campaign has
not established the intended neural economic or computational advantage. The re-
search objective remains a competitive learned recursive Bellman operator, with the
original model, strong controls and full decision costs determining that comparison.

The action bounds specify a concrete route for further algorithmic work. An
original derivative enclosure can stop regret certification when its capacity-sensitive
bound plus the future-policy allowance meets the economic tolerance. A proposed
policy change requires the original continuation contrast bound, including that
allowance, to certify improvement. Building these bounds from the learned critic
requires the feature-range and off-design calculations in Theorem S.7; the current
finite-node fitting audit does not provide them. The simultaneous event results
preserve both potential gains and harms across states, but they do not implement a
selection rule. Using independent evaluation labels to choose the favorable actions
afterwards would give the selector information and cost treatment absent from the
frozen experiment.
Precision allocation must therefore be tied to a decision that the additional in-
formation can resolve. Taking closer finite-difference probes while leaving the
value enclosures unchanged can amplify uncertainty through division by the probe
distance. Increasing the state grid also costs more without guaranteeing a better
feasible action, as the complete budget comparison shows. The proved path and
stationarity conditions identify valid stopping tests; the cost of acquiring them,
the choice of refinement and a safe deployable selector remain to be demonstrated
under a new independent protocol. The existing probe radius, grids, models and
evaluation states are unchanged by this interpretation. Risk integration and the
state-dependent anchor remain essential when an operator is used recursively.
The acquisition budgets in this experiment change information density and repre-
sentation size within the same two-state economy. They do not establish scalability
in horizon, state dimension or innovation dimension. The retained theorems de-
scribe those separate objects and their assumptions; their historical experiments
and unresolved regions remain in the development companion. The stopping,
accuracy-allocation and risk-information questions therefore remain part of the
NBO programme under the original economic criteria.
A neural-specific advantage requires a distinction that a conventional method
with the same information, features, feasible policies and resources cannot re-
produce. The exactly matched hinge control makes one such boundary explicit.
Conditional adoption additionally requires the original objective gain to pay for

empirical and mathematical requirements for an economically useful NBO, not
consequences of a successful optimization status or a smaller internal loss.
The measured ReLU–hinge comparison needs a further computational distinction.
The two encodings carry identical mathematical features and readouts. Under
the frozen acquisition procedure, the coordinate-loop hinge implementation pays
for the corresponding ReLU fit and its own encoding, identity check and audit.
Those are real costs of the executed implementation, and remain in the ledger. A
conventional hinge representation can also use the same batched evaluation and
elementary operations as the ReLU implementation. Consequently a cost difference
caused by the declared copy or evaluation procedure cannot establish a neural-
specific computational advantage. Any sufficient price region against the recorded
implementations is conditional on that measured menu. Its interpretation must
also retain the other strong conventional alternatives and the distinction between
implementation cost and a limitation of conventional representation.

AA.5. Machine tables and exact record custody
The machine companion retains all 3,712 state-level economic rows and every
original key; the 56 independent fit audits and their exact finite-design gaps; all
1,624 unordered full-menu original-objective comparisons (812 for all64 and 812
for the first32); all 348 clock and counter records; all 9,280 timing identity checks;
all actual first and rejected candidates, root traces and qualification stages; 1,392
complete volume-cost/frontier rows; every individual pairwise price constraint;
2,832 full or within-budget menu regions and 472 five-clock intersections. Empty,
adverse and inconclusive cases are included. Not being certifiably dominated by
these interval records does not prove membership of the unknown exact economic
frontier.
The output manifest lists every deterministic replay file. Execution duration,
absolute input locations, file metadata and the evolving publication/support ledger
are separate custody products, excluded from byte-identical scientific-table replay
with that exclusion stated explicitly. The frozen scientific files, actor artifact M and
state artifact D are checked against immutable Git objects before reporting. This
program imports no production economic primitive, training solver or evaluator
and does not reacquire, refit, redraw, resolve an economic action or retime a service.

APPENDIX AB: RETAINED COMPLETE R120 MAIN-ARTICLE ACCOUNT
The following R120 introduction, numerical study and conclusions retain their
original source bytes and execution identity. Their policy-improvement statements
and full proofs are preserved across the technical supplement and this companion,
with exact source routes recorded in the retention map. Occurrences of “current”,
“new” and “this experiment” inside retained inputs refer to the revision that origi-
nally wrote them.
APPENDIX AC: INTRODUCTION
An economic decision rule must choose a feasible action using the information
available at the decision date. Its numerical value is determined by the resulting
recursive economic objective and by the resources needed to deliver that action.
Neural Bellman Operators (NBOs) study the construction and learning of continua-
tion operators for this purpose. A learned critic represents the continuation entering
a Bellman problem; an actor obtains an admissible decision from that represented
problem; and the value of the implemented policy follows its own future decisions
under the original economic recursion. This distinction becomes consequential with
nonlinear recursive risk, state-dependent action constraints, imperfect optimization,
and finite information acquisition.
The central question is when learning a continuation operator improves eco-
nomic decisions at a competitive complete cost. Answering it requires more than
a function-approximation result. A small fitted value residual can coexist with a
poor action direction, an incorrect boundary decision, an expensive risk evalua-
tion, or an uncertified future policy. A representation that is cheap to query can
also be expensive to acquire or to qualify. The original NBO framework therefore
keeps the target Bellman recursion, the implemented policy recursion, and the
computational account explicit. This revision advances that framework through
action comparisons whose information requirements depend on the actions being
compared, followed by a new original-objective policy-improvement study.
Our principal application is the original constrained investment economy. A firm
has a vector of productive states, a state-dependent investment capacity, a nonlinear

propagation technology, and continuous innovations. Current and terminal costs
penalize distance from productive targets, cross-component imbalances, and severe
aggregate shortfalls. Upper-tail cost risk is evaluated recursively, so the adverse
continuation distribution affects the investment decision at each date. The model
has a uniquely defined original Bellman optimum and a measurable implemented
terminal controller. These objects permit economic comparisons of neural, hinge,
polynomial, spline, grid and semi-analytic continuations using one original ob-
jective and feasible action set, with common access to the economic primitives.
The application is a controlled economic numerical experiment; its cost units and
initial-state distribution are declared rather than estimated from empirical firm
data.
An action-scaled Bellman comparison.
The first contribution is a quantitative com-
parison modulus derived from the original constrained technology and recursive
preference. Let fa(z) = V1(F(x, a, z)) denote the original optimal continuation after
action a. For the two-dimensional investment problem we prove a global Lipschitz
bound Mα for the state gradient of V1, including binding investment constraints and
changes of the active risk tail. Normalizing the feasible action interval makes the
boundary calculation explicit. It follows that Lip( fb −fa) ≤(4/5)Mα|b −a|. Thus
the fixed-density integration error of the continuation difference admits a bound
proportional to action distance, even when the level of each continuation remains
substantial.
This modulus gives a computable paired midpoint interval. Intersecting it with
the separately valid convex midpoint–secant intervals yields the integration width
min{2KR(1 −α)n−2, EabR(1 −α)n−1},
Eab = (4/5)Mα|b −a|,
under a known feasible risk-tail density and exact point information. Acquired node
errors, numerical accumulation, tail localization and future-policy error are then
charged explicitly. We prove a matching worst-case order for a precise fixed-density
scalar-value information interface. The comparison applies to all representations
given that interface. The additional smoothness and algebraic access available in

The second contribution connects action alignment to the movement of the ad-
verse tail. A common feasible density has a nonnegative deficit relative to the
maximizing density of each continuation. Strong convexity in the innovation and
the action-scaled comparison modulus transfer a bound for one deficit to the other,
including a tail optimizer at the boundary. At an exactly optimal candidate tail, the
resulting mismatch allowance is quadratic in action distance. The implemented
comparison keeps both directly acquired deficits and intersects the incumbent
deficit with this transfer bound. It retains the original risk supremum throughout.
A policy change must improve the implemented policy.
The new gate starts from a
completed, qualified incumbent. A candidate is accepted only when its original
complete-policy contrast has a strictly negative upper bound and the candidate satis-
fies the unchanged original regret and interval-width requirements. Every accepted
step therefore has a certified economic gain. Every refusal, unresolved comparison,
and proposal acquisition remains in the cost account. The three projected support
proposals and the completed-incumbent safeguard are retained methods; the new
numerical mechanism changes the information used to authorize their realized
policy changes.
We prove a finite-resolution sufficient condition for acceptance, with distinct
allowances for common-tail mismatch, point accuracy, integration, and actual future
behavior. There is also a sharp limit to the stated information: knowing the optimal-
future action values exactly leaves a comparison uncertainty of ±βε1 when the
implemented future policy is known only to have error in [0, ε1]. Resolving smaller
gains requires information about that actual future policy. This result identifies a
specific numerical research problem within NBO rather than treating an unresolved
comparison as optimality or interpreting additional internal fitting accuracy as
economic progress.

ates the original continuous terminal risk and also constructs an all-action lower
bound for the original date-zero optimum. This gives original policy regret and
action-distance bounds in addition to fixed-policy value enclosures. Prespecified bi-
nomial and bounded-mean inference transfer certified gains over each service’s own
incumbent to the declared state population. Cross-representation adoption still re-
quires comparing complete economic costs and all acquisition and decision-service
resources.
Relation to numerical control and learning.
Monotone improvement from approx-
imate policy evaluation has a substantial literature. Metelli et al. (2021) construct
policy-improvement lower bounds and safe policy-iteration schemes. Eshwar et al.
(2026) study Bellman-constrained evaluation and conservative improvement with
function approximation. These works make the general need for an improvement
guarantee clear. The present addition concerns the paid continuous-risk action-
comparison problem generated by the original NBO economy, its explicit con-
strained smoothness and tail-mismatch constants, and the policy consequences of
that information. Accuracy certificates for convex minimization with inexact oracles
also supply valid stopping criteria (Gladin et al., 2023). Here the economic recursion
requires separately accounting for continuation, risk, feasible actions, and the actual
future controller; an internal optimization residual alone does not provide those
accounts. Classical binomial inversion and concentration are attributed when used,

Supplement proves the Bellman foundations, stability, own-future errors, con-

for its prospectively declared study.

AE.3. Economic gains and the strong conventional comparison
The gains in Table AE.I concern a concrete investment decision. Investment
increases the two next-period stocks by a/2 and a/4, whereas the continuous in-
novation shifts them by (z,−z). The innovation therefore changes their imbalance
without changing their aggregate. The decision trades the convex current adjust-
ment cost against stock tracking, the low-stock penalty, the capacity constraint and
the original risk-sensitive continuation. At a common initial state, the current state
cost cancels from the comparison. It is the action-dependent continuation differ-
ence, together with the adjustment-cost difference, that must justify an intervention.
These are normalized original-objective units. The experiment supplies no monetary
or consumption-equivalent welfare calibration.
Numerical displays in this discussion summarize retained exact rational intervals;
the exact endpoints determine every sign and price condition. All seven learned
representations improve on their own completed incumbents at both risk levels
under each of L, P and D. The independent mean-gain lower bounds are strictly
positive in all 42 such cells. For ReLU, P and L return the same policies: the mean
original-policy gains are approximately [212.675,213.885] × 10−6 at α = 1/2 and
[162.411,163.501] × 10−6 at α = 3/4. The corresponding independent mean-regret
upper bounds fall from 215.906 to 2.626 and from 165.361 to 2.406, respectively, in
the same 10−6 units. The original-action RMS-error upper bounds fall from 0.01470

The magnitude of an improvement also depends on the initial actor’s quality. The
spline gains are larger than the ReLU gains because the completed spline incumbent
has a larger original loss in this catalogue. They do not establish a superior final
spline policy. More decisively, the online semi-analytic incumbent has a strictly

the 64 states at both risks. Its independent mean-regret upper bounds are already
1.898 × 10−6 and 1.851 × 10−6. Online also retains a strictly lower original objec-

[0.1506,1.2864] × 10−6 and [0.06473,1.0451] × 10−6 at the two risks. ReLU with D
reaches intervals overlapping the online policy, without resolving a strict mean
advantage. All 512 ReLU–hinge policy pairs are exactly identical, and both represen-
tations pay the complete learned-feature acquisition charge. This control rules out a
neural-specific policy advantage within the executed equal-feature comparison.
AE.4. What the new comparison changes
The comparison with inherited improvement is more demanding than the
comparison with an unrefined learned incumbent. P changes 391 of its 1024 re-
turned actions and accepts 815 strict improvement steps. L changes 388 actions
and accepts 807 steps. Their final actions differ on only 12 of the 1024 common
state/representation/risk cases. Nine of the 16 cell-level policy comparisons are
exact identities; all seven remaining independent mean-value intervals contain zero.
The retained intervals include both directions. Thus this experiment resolves gains
over learned incumbents while leaving the incremental mean economic advantage
of P over L unresolved.

policy difference upper bound is approximately −1.05403 × 10−5, whereas the

independent observations. The mixed upper is active at 5961 of 9016 paid preci-
sion levels, but is necessary for acceptance at only those two recorded levels. The
transferred incumbent tail-defect bound is inactive in all 2290 acquired density
pairs. Its theorem remains valid; no observed reduction in incumbent tail work is
attributed to it. These diagnostics establish use of the new comparison at a specified
paid resolution. They do not establish failure of a traditional method after a further
refinement or measure a counterfactual time saving.
The complete costs in Table AE.II impose a further qualification. P costs more
than L in every one of the 16 primary cells, with ratios from 1.143 to 1.821. It is also
slower in all 48 matched fresh clocks; their complete-cost ratios range from 1.048
to 2.040. All three clocks, including their different magnitudes, remain reported.
D is faster than P in every primary cell and all 48 matched clocks. Against L, D
is faster in 41 clocks and slower in seven, with 14 favorable and two adverse cell
medians. Its independent original-policy mean is strictly better than L and P in five
cells—ReLU and hinge at both risks, and spline at α = 3/4—with two exact online
identities and nine unresolved comparisons. The conventional direct proposal is
therefore an essential comparator to the new three-proposal rule.
Work counts and elapsed cost rank these procedures differently. Summed over the
same 16 cells, L purchases 2,032,754 compiled terminal rows, P purchases 1,758,340,
and D purchases 14,608,426. The corresponding sums of complete standalone 64-
state costs are 94.478, 132.729 and 80.302 seconds. P retains 2257 rejected candidate
attempts, including 785 exhausted precision ladders; D retains 633 rejections, includ-
ing 194 exhausted ladders. Identical-action shortcuts remain in these counts and are
distinguished from purchased precision levels. The price of a point-information in-
terface cannot be inferred from its point count alone. These measured results retain
separate compiler, proposal, risk-query and certificate counters and the actual co-
hort clocks; they do not combine overlapping counters into a universal information
unit or identify an unmeasured causal timing decomposition.

AE.5. Population scope and actual adoption conditions
The frozen population analysis supplies a positive mean-gain lower bound for
all 42 learned-incumbent comparisons, with the simultaneous event-and-mean
family coverage stated in Table AE.III. The event-staircase lower bounds range from
2.661 × 10−6 to 14.192 × 10−6. The ordinary bounded-mean lower bounds alone are
zero; the predeclared positive-gain events supply the positive lower conclusions.
The upper intervals remain broad. The six online comparisons have observed zero
gains and lower bound zero; the finite sample does not prove that refinement is
unnecessary everywhere. The inference concerns the declared finite-uniform initial-
state distribution conditional on frozen actors and the ideal independent entropy
assumption. It does not turn the 992 same-sample cross-representation contrasts
into a new population comparison family.
A gain over a weak incumbent can pay for refinement without making its rep-
resentation the preferred method. Using the actual 64-state workload and its own
acquisition-plus-cohort cost, P improves the cost-augmented ReLU incumbent mean
for computing prices in [0,0.001902379 . . .) at α = 1/2 and [0,0.001769390 . . .) at
α = 3/4, in original-objective units per second. The exact rational open endpoints,
not their printed decimal approximations, define these sets. Every one of the 32
ReLU comparisons against the full conventional menu, across the four predeclared
amortization volumes and after intersection across all three clocks, has an empty
sufficient-price set. The corresponding intersections of upper “not ruled out” con-
ditions are empty as well. At the individual-clock level, 12 of 96 ReLU/menu
upper-condition regions remain nonempty, all for direct refinement; the actual pri-
mary 64-state comparison has two such unresolved regions. These upper conditions
establish no sufficient adoption region, but preserve the cases that a single timing
scenario does not rule out. Across all representations, the 17 nonempty sufficient
menu-price regions belong to completed conventional policies. These are conditions
on the recorded sample and the declared cost scenario, not evidence of population
adoption or measured throughput scaling. When a cheaper policy has a worse orig-
inal objective, time savings can compensate only in the cost-augmented calculation;
they do not improve the unpriced original Bellman objective.

The deployment comparison includes actual production certificates, refused pro-
posals, acquisition, loading and cohort bookkeeping. The 64 primary cohort clocks
sum to 331.550 seconds; the complete primary process, including three timing
subprocesses and its other work, takes 841.861 seconds. The separate independent
rational reconstruction takes 1806.153 seconds and is paid as research validation
rather than silently assigned zero or amortized away in the deployment-price
formula. Source/artifact checks, imports, process startup and final receipt work
remain in the retained process and launcher ledger; they are not claimed as sepa-
rately measured per-arm cohort components. Acquisition-plus-cohort sums charge
standalone acquisition to each hypothetical deployment and therefore differ from
the actual shared acquisition process. The mathematical progress is a valid action-
dependent comparison and a certified rule that changes decisions under the original
objective. The completed evidence identifies the remaining computational task pre-
cisely: preserve that validity while reducing paid decision work relative to strong
conventional proposals and resolving advantages beyond ordinary equal-feature
representations. Figure AE.1 displays every cell of the incremental P/L comparison,
connecting the original-policy enclosures to all paid clocks.
APPENDIX AF: CONCLUSION
Neural Bellman Operators connect learned continuation operators to feasible
decisions and the economic value of their implemented future behavior. The con-
struction requires a fixed original recursion and a complete accounting of the
information used by its critic, actor and numerical certificate. The constrained
investment model makes these requirements explicit while retaining continuous
innovations and nonlinear recursive risk.
The new action-comparison theory uses the geometry of the original Bellman
problem. A constrained state-gradient modulus yields an action-scaled continuation-
difference bound; convex integration and a constrained risk-defect transfer then
provide computable comparison intervals. Qualification and a strict original-policy
improvement bound jointly govern replacement of a completed incumbent. The
proof also identifies what additional precision can resolve and what remains hidden

behind a uniform future-policy allowance. This distinction gives a concrete stopping
criterion and a specified information problem for subsequent NBO algorithms.
The independent experiment certifies gains over the completed learned incum-
bents under the original investment objective. All 42 learned-incumbent refinement
groups have positive simultaneous population mean-gain lower bounds; the in-
dependent optimum supports also give much smaller upper bounds on original
policy regret and root-mean-square optimal-action error. These gains coexist with a
strong online incumbent that is already close to optimal. The new paired service
changes twelve returned actions relative to inherited safe improvement, but no cell-
level incremental mean advantage is resolved, and all sixteen primary costs and all
forty-eight matched clocks are higher. The mixed comparison authorizes one shared
candidate at a recorded resolution where the separate convex bound is inconclu-
sive. The direct conventional proposal has a strictly lower independently enclosed
sample mean cost than both L and P in five cells and is faster than P throughout the
matched clocks. ReLU and hinge policies are identical. ReLU has empty sufficient
full-menu adoption regions, and its upper-condition intersections across the three
timing scenarios are empty; individual-clock upper conditions leave some cases
unresolved. These findings preserve the independent neural contribution as an
explicit scientific problem.
The remaining research priorities concern the joint design of continuation learning
and paid economic decisions. They include acquisition losses that reduce action-
comparison work, information about the actual future controller that resolves
gains below the present allowance, and matched experiments with longer horizons,
multiple controls and higher-dimensional continuous risk. The retained stochastic-
control, recursive-utility and stopped-boundary results provide separate rigorous
foundations for this program. Progress on these problems must preserve the original
objective, give conventional methods the same usable information, and demonstrate
the economic value of the resulting policies together with their full computational
cost.

APPENDIX AJ: RETAINED COMPLETE R119 MAIN-ARTICLE ACCOUNT
The following R119 framing, numerical-service details and empirical comparisons
are retained byte-for-byte in their original source inputs. Their execution identity is
distinct from the new R120 policy-improvement experiment. The R119 continuous-
risk information theorem remains in the current main article.
APPENDIX AK: INTRODUCTION
Dynamic investment under risk requires a continuation value, a feasible action,
and a decision about how much information to acquire before acting. A small
continuation fitting error need not imply a small decision loss. It can move a nearly
binding action, alter the adverse innovation tail, or leave an expensive original-
model verification problem unresolved. Neural Bellman Operators (NBOs) study
these objects together: recursively constructed and learned continuation maps
propose policies, their own future decisions determine policy value, and original-
law Bellman inequalities qualify the actions actually delivered.
The economic question is when an acquired neural continuation helps deliver
original-objective decisions at a competitive complete cost. Answering it requires
conventional representations with the same information, feasible actions and numer-
ical components. A conventional hinge encoding of the same ReLU map receives
the same policy and certificate. A quadratic continuation that wins a complete-work
comparison remains a successful control. The purpose of these comparisons is to
identify which part of continuation construction, information acquisition and policy
improvement creates economic value.
This paper develops a chain from recursive continuation construction to action-
aligned information and verified decisions. The retained own-future NBO construc-
tion gives an exactly realizable neural continuation and a measurable feasible actor
without assuming successful nonconvex training. Centered recursive-risk inequal-
ities separate irrelevant value-level shifts from action-dependent approximation
errors. Original-model supporting quadratics then connect the realized constrained
action to the original Bellman optimum. The assumptions behind Bellman existence,
measurability, continuity and uniqueness are stated explicitly; the supplement

proves them for compact innovation supports and verifies the original investment

Nonlinear risk introduces an economic obstacle beyond directional fitting error.
Even when two continuations have identical action derivatives at every innovation,
their maximizing risk densities can differ. The retained continuous-law tail-switch
example has zero directional approximation error and original action loss 1/4.
Centered quantile-band bounds identify the additional near-tail information needed
to control this discrepancy. The present addition determines how much point
information is needed to resolve that tail, and constructs a policy certificate when
its location is only approximately known.
For a convex K-Lipschitz continuation on [−R, R] under the original uniform law,
an adverse tail of probability t = 1 −α consists of at most two endpoint intervals. Its
complement is a central interval of fixed length. The derivative of the integral over
that central interval is the difference between two endpoint continuation values; it is
monotone and Lipschitz. Consequently paid bisection locates the relevant tails, and
midpoint–secant integration can concentrate on their total length 2Rt. Including
every localization query, we prove a deterministic worst-case risk-width upper
bound of order KRtN−2. Together with a fully restated indistinguishability lower
bound, this gives matching risk-level dependence for N ≥32. This resolves the
factor t−1 in the retained whole-support upper account. The theorem specifies exact
point information; bit precision and the work needed to obtain each continuation
value have their own implementation account.
The original nonlinear investment economy supplies an implementable version.
Primitive curvature implies that the optimal continuation along its innovation
direction is strongly convex with modulus 181/64. For any proposed feasible tail
cut, outward intervals for the two endpoint values bound its failure to maximize
the original risk functional by a constrained quadratic calculation. This defect is
paid explicitly. The same fixed feasible density and global continuation supports
produce a lower bound over the entire original action interval. Selected-tail secants
and the unchanged implemented-future allowance produce an upper bound on the
actual complete policy. No derivative through a rounded actor, fitted sign assertion
or hypothetical future optimizer obtains certificate authority.
